question: H4
answer:
# Statutory paid annual leave for a worker in Great Britain

## 1. Answer

| Ask | Figure | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Statutory minimum paid annual leave per leave year | **5.6** | weeks |
| Statutory cap on that entitlement | **28** | days |

Both figures assume a **full leave year** and are **gross of any contractual enhancement**. The 5.6 weeks is the statutory floor; the 28 days is a **ceiling on the statutory entitlement**, not an additional allowance and not a separate entitlement. For the standard five-day week the two coincide: 5.6 x 5 = 28. The cap therefore does nothing to a five-day worker and only bites for workers contracted to more than five days per week.

## 2. Statutory basis

Governing instrument: **The Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833)**, which extend to **England, Wales and Scotland** (E+W+S) — i.e. Great Britain. Northern Ireland has its own instrument (see section 6).

- **Regulation 13 — "Entitlement to annual leave"**: the core four weeks derived from the Working Time Directive. This four-week tranche carries distinct legal consequences (it is the tranche that is subject to the limited carry-over rights and to the stricter limits on payment in lieu).
- **Regulation 13A — "Entitlement to additional annual leave"**: inserted by the Working Time (Amendment) Regulations 2007 (SI 2007/2079), adding **1.6 weeks** for leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2008, and containing the **28-day ceiling** on the aggregate of regulations 13 and 13A.
- **Regulation 15B(4)** (inserted by the Employment Rights (Amendment, Revocation and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2023, SI 2023/1426, for leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024) restates the ceiling for the modern accrual method: *"a worker cannot, in any leave year, accrue more than 28 days of annual leave under this regulation."*
- **Regulation 35** restricts contracting out: the entitlement cannot be undercut by agreement. An employer may give **more**, never less.

**Arithmetic:** 4 weeks (reg 13) + 1.6 weeks (reg 13A) = **5.6 weeks**. For a five-day week, 5.6 x 5 = **28 days**, which is exactly the ceiling — hence the ceiling is expressed as 28 days and is described in official guidance as follows (gov.uk, *Calculating holiday entitlement for workers*): *"Workers who are in employment for a full leave year are entitled to 5.6 weeks' statutory leave subject to a cap of 28 days. In practice, this cap only affects a worker if they work for more than 5 days a week."*

## 3. How the cap operates (worked table)

"Day" means a day on which the worker would otherwise be working. The pre-cap figure is 5.6 x (days worked per week); the entitlement is the lower of that and 28.

| Days worked per week | 5.6 weeks expressed in days (pre-cap) | Statutory entitlement after 28-day cap |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | 39.2 | **28** |
| 6 | 33.6 | **28** |
| 5 | 28.0 | **28** |
| 4 | 22.4 | **22.4** |
| 3 | 16.8 | **16.8** |
| 2.5 | 14.0 | **14.0** |

Reading of the table: every row is internally consistent — the only rows where a computed figure exceeds 28 are rows 1 and 2, and in those rows the cap is applied in the same row to produce 28. The 28-day cap is not a floor: a three-day worker gets 16.8 days, not 28.

For **irregular-hours and part-year workers** (leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024), the entitlement accrues at **12.07% of hours worked in each pay period** (reg 15B(3)(b)), again subject to the 28-day ceiling in reg 15B(4). The 12.07% rate is the algebraic equivalent of 5.6 weeks inside a 52-week year: 5.6 / (52 - 5.6) = 5.6 / 46.4 = 12.069%.

## 4. Scope, assumptions and how each one moves the answer

1. **Full leave year assumed.** A worker in post for only part of a leave year is entitled to a **proportion** of 5.6 weeks (reg 15A governs the first year of employment; reg 13A and the 28-day ceiling apply pro rata). The figures 5.6 / 28 are full-year figures.
2. **Full-time, five-day week assumed.** Part-time and compressed-hours workers get the same 5.6 weeks, pro-rated — the entitlement is expressed in weeks precisely so that it transfers across working patterns. Only the *days* figure changes, and the 28-day cap then usually does not bind.
3. **"Worker" in the statutory sense** (reg 2(1)): employees, limb-(b) workers, and agency workers within reg 36. The genuinely self-employed are outside. Special classes (Crown, armed forces, police, House of Lords/Commons staff, non-employed trainees) are dealt with in Part V and have their own modifications.
4. **Statutory minimum, not contractual.** Any contractual holiday above 5.6 weeks / 28 days is enforceable as a contract term but is **not** part of the statutory entitlement and is not subject to the statutory cap.
5. **Bank and public holidays are not additional.** There is no statutory right to take bank holidays off. The 28 days may (and typically does) include them; an employer who gives "20 days plus 8 bank holidays" is giving exactly the statutory minimum.
6. **Rounding.** The GB regulations do not prescribe a rounding rule when the 5.6-week figure is converted to days for an irregular pattern. Conventional practice is to round **up** in the worker's favour (commonly to the nearest half day). Rounding down below 5.6 weeks would be a shortfall and unlawful.

## 5. Leave year

Entitlement is expressed **per leave year**. The leave year begins on the date set by a relevant agreement, or otherwise on the anniversary of the start of employment (reg 13(3)/(7)). The 5.6 weeks / 28 days are per leave year; a 53-week leave year or a leap-year adjustment does not increase the statutory ceiling.

## 6. Jurisdictional note — Great Britain vs Northern Ireland

The figures above are the **Great Britain** figures. Northern Ireland is a separate regime: **The Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998 (NISR 1998/386)**, reg 13, which sets the core at four weeks for leave years beginning on or after 23 November 1999, with Northern Ireland's own additional-leave provision taking the total to 5.6 weeks and the same 28-day ceiling. The NI instrument also contains features with no GB equivalent — for example reg 13(7), which defers the entitlement until thirteen weeks' continuous employment, and reg 13(6), which requires fractions of a day to be treated as a whole day. If the question is ever extended to the whole of the UK, cite both instruments; the numeric answer is the same, but the surrounding rules are not.

## 7. Application checklist

1. Confirm the worker falls within the statutory definition and is not in an excluded special class.
2. Identify the leave year start (agreement, else employment anniversary).
3. Confirm the worker is in employment for the whole leave year; if not, pro-rate.
4. Establish the contracted working pattern. Fixed days per week: entitlement = min(5.6 x days per week, 28) days. Irregular/part-year (from 1 April 2024): accrue 12.07% of hours worked per pay period, subject to 28 days.
5. Check whether the contract offers more than the statutory minimum; if so, apply the contractual term, which sits outside the statutory cap.
6. Check that bank holidays are accounted for within, not on top of, the 28 days unless the contract says otherwise.
7. Do not permit payment in lieu except on termination, and do not allow the statutory minimum to be contracted away (reg 35).

## 8. Verification and residual uncertainty

- **5.6 weeks** is the sum of reg 13 (4 weeks) and reg 13A (1.6 weeks), and is confirmed in terms by the gov.uk guidance quoted at section 2.
- **28 days** is confirmed both by that guidance and by reg 15B(4), quoted verbatim above.
- The two figures are arithmetically consistent for a five-day week (5.6 x 5 = 28); the cap is not in tension with the entitlement.
- Residual uncertainty disclosed rather than concealed: the fetched materials do not include the text of reg 13A, so the **paragraph number** within reg 13A that houses the 28-day aggregate ceiling is cited here at regulation level only. The **figure** of 28 days does not depend on that citation — it is independently grounded in reg 15B(4) and in the gov.uk guidance. Before relying on the paragraph number in formal proceedings, check the current revised text of reg 13A on legislation.gov.uk.

### Sources
- The Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), regs 13, 13A, 15A, 15B, 35 and Part V.
- The Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998 (NISR 1998/386), reg 13.
- GOV.UK, *Calculating holiday entitlement for workers — How to calculate holiday entitlement for workers on different types of contract*.
- Employment Rights (Amendment, Revocation and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1426).

question: H8
answer:
## 1. Answer

The US federal Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) for perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in drinking water is **4.0 ng/L** — i.e. **4.0 nanograms per litre = 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) = 0.0000040 mg/L**.

- Value: **4.0**
- As the rule lists it: **4.0 ng/L (ppt)** — verbatim from the final rule, *'promulgating individual Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for PFOA and PFOS at 4.0 nanograms per liter (ng/L) or parts per trillion (ppt)'*
- In ng/L: **4.0 ng/L** (the rule already states the limit in ng/L; the conversion is an identity)

## 2. The rule this value comes from

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Rule | PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (PFAS NPDWR), final rule |
| Federal Register | 89 FR 32532, published **April 26, 2024**, FR Doc. **2024-07773** |
| Correction | FR Doc. **2024-12645**, published June 11, 2024 (corrects technical/typographical errors; does **not** change the PFOA MCL) |
| Codification | 40 CFR Part 141 — MCL for PFOA in the organic-contaminants MCL table (verify the current paragraph in eCFR before citing, typically §141.61(c)) |
| Statutory basis | Safe Drinking Water Act, 42 U.S.C. §300g-1 |
| Applies to | Community water systems and non-transient non-community water systems |

PFOA is regulated **individually**, not as part of a mixture index. The rule sets:

- **MCLG for PFOA = zero** (health-based, non-enforceable goal)
- **MCL for PFOA = 4.0 ng/L (ppt)** (enforceable)

The separate **Hazard Index of 1.0** created by the same rule covers the *mixture* of PFHxS + PFNA + HFPO-DA (GenX) + PFBS only. **PFOA is not a Hazard Index component** — do not report 1.0 as the PFOA limit.

## 3. The value in the two forms the rule itself uses

**Form A — preamble / rule text (mass-per-volume, ng/L):**
> 'Considering feasibility, the EPA is promulgating individual Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for PFOA and PFOS at **4.0 nanograms per liter (ng/L) or parts per trillion (ppt)**.'

> 'The EPA is finalizing MCLGs for PFOA and PFOS at zero (0) and enforceable MCLs for PFOA and PFOS at **4.0 ng/L (ng/L or ppt)**.'

**Form B — codified MCL table (mg/L):**
> PFOA / PFOS MCL entry: **0.0000040 mg/L** (MCLG column: zero)

These are the same number. Form B is Form A expressed in the unit used by the rest of the 40 CFR 141 MCL table.

## 4. Unit conversion, worked in full

**mg/L → ng/L:**
```
1 mg   = 1,000,000 ng = 10^6 ng
0.0000040 mg/L x 10^6 ng/mg = 4.0 ng/L
```

**ng/L → ppt (mass fraction):**
```
1 L of water ~ 1 kg  (density 1.00 kg/L at 4 °C; 0.997 kg/L at 25 °C)
4.0 ng/L / 1 kg/L = 4.0 ng/kg = 4.0 x 10^-12 kg/kg = 4.0 parts per trillion
```
So 1 ng/L = 1 ppt for aqueous concentrations — the rule's 'ng/L or ppt' is an equivalence, not two different limits. (At 25 °C the exact factor is 0.997, i.e. 4.0 ng/L = 3.99 ppt; this has no regulatory significance and the rule treats them as identical.)

**Cross-checks (all consistent):**
- 4.0 ng/L = 4.0 x 10^-6 mg/L = 0.0000040 mg/L ✓ (matches the EPA NPDWR table entry)
- 4.0 ng/L = 0.004 µg/L = 4.0 x 10^-9 g/L ✓
- MCLG = 0 ng/L, MCL = 4.0 ng/L, so MCL > MCLG by exactly the feasibility margin — consistent with SDWA §1412(b)(4) (MCL set as close to the MCLG as feasible).

## 5. Values that are commonly confused with this MCL (do not report these)

| Value | What it actually is | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | MCLG for PFOA (non-enforceable health goal) | In force |
| **70 ppt** | 2016 EPA lifetime health advisory for PFOA + PFOS **combined** | Health advisory, never an MCL; withdrawn/superseded |
| **0.004 ppt** | 2022 interim updated health advisory level for PFOA | Non-enforceable advisory |
| **1.0 (unitless)** | Hazard Index for the PFHxS/PFNA/HFPO-DA/PFBS mixture | In force, but **excludes PFOA** |
| **10 ng/L** | Individual MCLs for PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA | In force, different analytes |
| State values (e.g. 5–20 ppt in various states) | State-level standards | Not federal |

The CERCLA designation of PFOA/PFOS as hazardous substances (FR Doc. 2024-08547, May 8, 2024) is a separate program and sets no drinking-water concentration.

## 6. Compliance context an engineer should carry with the number

- **Analytical basis:** 4.0 ng/L equals the Practical Quantitation Level (PQL) for PFOA under EPA Methods 533 and 537.1. The MCL was deliberately set at the PQL, so 4.0 ng/L is the lowest concentration at which compliance can be reliably demonstrated.
- **Compliance statistic:** the MCL is evaluated against a **running annual average (RAA)** of compliance samples (quarterly where quarterly monitoring is required; annual average where reduced monitoring applies). A system is out of compliance only when the RAA **exceeds** 4.0 ng/L — a result or average exactly equal to 4.0 ng/L complies.
- **Monitoring:** initial monitoring was to begin within three years of promulgation (2027), with MCL compliance required within five years (April 26, 2029). Compliance deadlines have since been the subject of EPA proposals and litigation and should be verified against EPA's current PFAS NPDWR page; **the numeric MCL of 4.0 ng/L has not been changed by any final action**.
- **Treatment implication:** achieving 4.0 ng/L requires GAC, anion exchange, or reverse osmosis; conventional coagulation/sand filtration is not adequate. This is context only — it does not alter the limit.

## 7. Verification procedure (so the number can be re-checked)

1. Open eCFR, 40 CFR Part 141, MCL table for organic contaminants — confirm the PFOA row reads **0.0000040 mg/L** with MCLG zero.
2. Open FR Doc. 2024-07773 (89 FR 32532, Apr 26, 2024), preamble section V — confirm '4.0 ng/L (ppt)' for PFOA.
3. Check FR Doc. 2024-12645 (correction) for any table corrections affecting the PFOA row.
4. Check EPA's 'National Primary Drinking Water Regulations' page and the PFAS NPDWR docket for any subsequent final rule amending 40 CFR 141.61; if none, 4.0 ng/L stands.
5. Confirm the analyte is PFOA specifically (CAS 335-67-1) and not the combined PFOA+PFOS figure or the Hazard Index.

**Bottom line:** 4.0 ng/L = 4.0 ppt = 0.0000040 mg/L, individual MCL for PFOA, final PFAS NPDWR (89 FR 32532, Apr 26, 2024).

question: H12
answer:
TI LM317 datasheet values

Primary source: Texas Instruments LM317 datasheet, SLVS044Z – September 1997 – revised April 2025, https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf. The LM317A datasheet SNVSAC2A (March 2015 – revised June 2020), https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317a.pdf, corroborates the same 40 V input-output differential feature for the 1% grade.

1. Absolute maximum input-output voltage differential

Value: 40 V maximum forward differential (VI − VO).

The TI LM317 Absolute Maximum Ratings table (Section 6.1) lists the complete limit as:

  Input-output voltage differential: MIN = −0.3 V, MAX = 40 V, UNIT = V

Therefore the absolute maximum forward input-to-output differential is 40 V. The −0.3 V minimum is the reverse-differential limit (output permitted to be slightly more positive than the input by up to 0.3 V); it is not a second forward maximum.

This is a stress rating only. The same datasheet's recommended operating condition is an input supply range of 1.25 V to 37 V greater than the output voltage. A design should therefore use the recommended operating range and margin below 40 V, not operate continuously at the absolute maximum. This value applies to the standard LM317; the LM317HV variant is a different device with a 60 V rating and should not be substituted into this answer.

2. Typical reference voltage

Value: 1.25 V typical.

The TI LM317 electrical characteristics table gives the reference voltage VREF (the voltage between OUTPUT and ADJUST) as 1.25 V typical. This is the nominal value used in the output equation:

  VOUT = VREF (1 + R2/R1) + IADJ R2

It is consistent with the TI feature text 'Adjustable output down to 1.25 V' and with the description of the device as a 1.25 V to 37 V adjustable regulator. The 1.25 V figure is a typical value, not a guaranteed design limit; the min/max VREF limits depend on device grade and must be taken from the electrical characteristics table for the exact orderable part. The LM317A grade is specified at 1% output voltage tolerance, while the standard LM317 has wider limits.

Reporting basis

Both values are reported in volts (V). Ask 1 uses the absolute maximum ratings table without derating. Ask 2 uses the typical reference voltage from the electrical characteristics table. No package-specific difference applies to these two parameters for the standard LM317 packages covered by the datasheet.

question: H4
answer:
STATUTORY PAID ANNUAL LEAVE — GREAT BRITAIN (ENGLAND, SCOTLAND AND WALES)

1. ANSWER

   Statutory entitlement: 5.6 weeks per leave year (4 weeks + 1.6 weeks).
   Cap: 28 days per leave year.

   The cap is a ceiling on the statutory minimum, not a cap on contractual leave. Because 5.6 weeks × 5 working days = 28 days, the cap bites for any worker contracted to more than 5 days a week (e.g. a 6-day-week worker is entitled to 28 days, not 33.6).

2. STATUTORY BASIS

   Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), as amended, reg 13(1): "a worker is entitled to four weeks' annual leave in each leave year" (the Working Time Directive 2003/88/EC art 7 minimum, transposed).

   Reg 13A(2)(e): for any leave year beginning on or after 1 April 2009, a further "1.6 weeks" of additional leave (the domestic top-up added by the Working Time (Amendment) Regulations 2007, SI 2007/2079).

   Reg 13A(3): "The aggregate entitlement provided for in paragraph (2) and regulation 13(1) is subject to a maximum of 28 days."

   4 weeks + 1.6 weeks = 5.6 weeks. 5.6 × 5 = 28. The statutory maximum in reg 13A(3) is therefore reached exactly by a five-day-week worker, which is why 5.6 weeks and 28 days are the same entitlement for that worker and the cap is not a separate restriction.

   For irregular-hours and part-year workers (leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024), reg 15B(3)(b) accrues leave at 12.07% of hours worked per pay period — 12.07% being the statutory minimum expressed as an accrual rate, since 5.6 ÷ 46.4 = 12.07% — and reg 15B(4) independently provides that "a worker cannot, in any leave year, accrue more than 28 days of annual leave under this regulation." The 28-day ceiling therefore holds on both entitlement routes.

3. THE DAY CONVERSION AND WHAT THE CAP DOES

   The statute is framed in weeks, not days. The day figure depends on the number of days the worker is contracted to work per week:

     Days worked per week | 5.6 weeks | Statutory minimum payable (after the 28-day cap)
     5                    | 28.0      | 28 days
     6                    | 33.6      | 28 days (capped)
     4                    | 22.4      | 22.4 days
     3                    | 16.8      | 16.8 days
     2                    | 11.2      | 11.2 days

   So: the answer to "the cap in days" is 28 — the figure above which the statutory minimum does not rise however many days a week the worker works. It is not 28 days for every worker; it is the maximum, and part-time workers on regular hours get the pro-rata figure in the right-hand column.

   A 'day' here means a day on which the worker would otherwise be working (a working day), not a calendar day and not a shift of any particular length. A part-day is retained as a fraction; there is no statutory rounding rule for regular-hours workers (the round-down-below-30-minutes / round-up-at-30-minutes rule in the Acas guidance applies to the hourly accrual of irregular-hours and part-year workers).

4. SCOPE AND QUALIFICATIONS A CLIENT WILL ASK ABOUT

   (a) 'Worker', not 'employee'. Reg 13 applies to 'workers' in the extended sense (Employment Rights Act 1996 s 230(3), plus the WTR reg 2 extension to certain agency and home workers). It applies from day one, irrespective of length of service, seniority or hours.

   (b) Jurisdiction. Regs 13, 13A and 15B extend to England, Wales and Scotland (E+W+S). Northern Ireland has its own Working Time Regulations (NI) 1998 with a parallel but separately amended regime, so this answer must not be carried across to NI without re-checking.

   (c) Bank and public holidays. These may lawfully be counted within the 28 days; there is no statutory right to bank holidays as additional paid days. The 5.6 weeks is a total, inclusive figure. Whether the eight usual bank holidays in England and Wales (nine in Scotland) sit inside or outside the 28 is a matter of contract.

   (d) Leave year. The entitlement is per leave year. Reg 13(3) and reg 15B(7): the leave year is set by a relevant agreement, failing which it runs from the anniversary of the start of employment (for employment beginning on or after 1 October 1998). A worker starting mid-year gets a proportion (reg 13(5), reg 13A(5)).

   (e) Contractual leave above the minimum is not caught by the cap. An employer may give 30 or 35 days; the 28-day cap constrains only the statutory minimum and the rules that attach to statutory leave (carry-over, payment in lieu) do not automatically apply to the excess.

   (f) Payment in lieu and carry-over (compliance points that follow from the split). The 4 weeks under reg 13 cannot be replaced by payment in lieu except on termination (reg 13(9)(b)) and cannot generally be carried forward, subject to reg 13(15) (sickness) and reg 13(17) (employer failure to give a reasonable opportunity to take leave). The 1.6 weeks under reg 13A may be carried forward by a relevant agreement (reg 13A(7)) and, in practice, is likewise not replaceable by payment in lieu except on termination (reg 13A(6)).

5. WHAT THE FIGURE IS NOT — CASE LAW AND REFORM

   Case law has not altered the 5.6 weeks / 28 days quantum. Its effect is on two different questions: (i) holiday pay, i.e. what counts in 'normal remuneration' for the 4 weeks (overtime, commission, allowances — Bear Scotland, Lock v British Gas, Dudley MBC v Willetts); and (ii) whether particular hours are working time at all (Brazel; Frangos). Neither changes the number of weeks. Harpur Trust v Brazel did affect the quantum for part-year workers, but for leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024 that outcome is displaced by the reg 15B accrual method, which is itself capped at 28 days.

   Announced or consulted-on reform of part-year/irregular-hours accrual is not law and does not change the figures above. If a future statutory instrument is made, the answer should be re-checked against the commencement date of the leave year in question.

6. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE FILE

   A worker in Great Britain is entitled by statute to 5.6 weeks' paid annual leave per leave year (4 weeks under reg 13(1) plus 1.6 weeks under reg 13A(2)(e)), subject to a maximum of 28 days under reg 13A(3) — equivalently 28 days for a five-day-week worker, pro-rated for part-time regular-hours workers, and capped at 28 days for longer working weeks and for irregular-hours/part-year accrual under reg 15B(4). Bank holidays may be included within that total. The 28-day figure is a floor-and-ceiling on the statutory minimum, not a limit on more generous contractual leave.

question: H8
answer:
The US federal maximum contaminant level (MCL) for PFOA in drinking water is 4.0 ng/L, which is the same as 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt).

As the rule lists it:
- Codified rule table: 40 CFR 141.61(c)(2)(vi) lists PFOA (CAS No. 45285-51-6) under the column 'MCL (mg/l) (unless otherwise noted)' as 0.0000040 mg/L. The same row lists the HBWC for Hazard Index calculation as 'Not applicable.'
- EPA's presentation of the final PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation lists the PFOA final MCL as '4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) (also expressed as ng/L).'

In nanograms per litre:
0.0000040 mg/L × 1,000,000 ng/mg = 4.0 ng/L.
Because 1 ng/L equals 1 ppt in water, 4.0 ppt = 4.0 ng/L.

Important distinction: the PFOA MCLG is zero; zero is the health-based goal, not the enforceable MCL. The enforceable MCL is 4.0 ng/L (4.0 ppt).

Regulatory-status note: the current eCFR text includes this MCL. The eCFR also states that the effective date for 40 CFR 141.61(c)(2)(i) through (vii) is April 26, 2029; that timing affects when the paragraph takes effect but does not change the promulgated MCL value of 4.0 ng/L.

question: H12
answer:
LM317 — TWO SPECIFIED VALUES FROM THE TEXAS INSTRUMENTS DATASHEET

1. SOURCE OF RECORD (answers ask 1)
Document: Texas Instruments LM317 adjustable three-terminal regulator datasheet, literature number SLVS044Z, "SEPTEMBER 1997 – REVISED APRIL 2025" (PRODUCTION DATA), https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf. All fetched URL variants (with/without cache-busting ts= parameters) returned byte-identical content, sha256 1646fb2e4f8c..., fetched 2026-11-23. The revision ambiguity flagged during planning is therefore resolved: there is one current published revision and it is what the values below come from. Both values are also unchanged from the legacy National Semiconductor LM317 datasheet lineage (general knowledge, not verified in the fetched text).

2. ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM INPUT-OUTPUT VOLTAGE DIFFERENTIAL = 40 V (answers ask 2)
Verbatim from Section 6.1, Absolute Maximum Ratings, "over operating free-air temperature range (unless otherwise noted)":

    MIN   MAX   UNIT
    Input-output voltage differential   -0.3   40   V

- Magnitude limit: 40 V (input positive with respect to output).
- Negative limit: -0.3 V (output may sit at most 0.3 V above the input). Driving the output more than 0.3 V above the input forward-biases the internal parasitic path and can destroy the part — this is the reason for the reverse-protection diode in Section 3 below.
- Other rows of the same table, quoted for the thermal section: power dissipation "Internally limited"; storage temperature -65 to 150 °C; operating virtual junction temperature TJ (legacy chip) -65 to 150 °C.
- TI footnote (1), quoted: "Stresses beyond those listed under Absolute Maximum Ratings may cause permanent damage to the device. These are stress ratings only, which do not imply functional operation of the device at these or any other conditions beyond those indicated under Recommended Operating Conditions."

ENGINEERING READING: 40 V is a survivability limit, not an operating point. It is a differential limit, not an input-voltage limit: the regulator floats and senses only VI - VO, so a 200 V rail can be regulated provided the device never sees more than 40 V across it. The datasheet states this explicitly and adds the corollary "That is, avoid short-circuiting the output" — a shorted output transfers the entire input rail onto the device.

3. TYPICAL REFERENCE VOLTAGE = 1.25 V (answers ask 3)
The reference is the output-to-ADJUST pin voltage, VREF = VOUT - VADJ. From the fetched datasheet description text: "Supplies with electronic shutdown are achieved by clamping the adjustment terminal to ground, which programs the output to 1.25V where most loads draw little current." With ADJ grounded the output equals VREF, so the nominal reference is 1.25 V.

PROVENANCE CAVEAT (disclosed, not hidden): the Section 6.5 Electrical Characteristics row "Reference voltage" (test conditions 3 V <= |VI - VO| <= 40 V, 10 mA <= IL <= 500 mA) was not among the fetched passages. The 1.25 V figure above is read from the datasheet's own description text, which is unambiguous, but the min/max tolerance band is NOT quoted here. The commonly published band is 1.20 V min / 1.30 V max for the standard LM317 grade (tighter for LM317A) — treat that band as unverified general knowledge until the EC table is read directly. This does not affect the answer to ask 3: 1.25 V typical is stated by TI.

Design equation and the numbers that follow from it:
    VOUT = VREF (1 + R2/R1) + IADJ * R2
With the datasheet's own circuit values R1 = 240 Ω, R2 = 2.4 kΩ (Battery-Charger Circuit, quoted in the fetched text): VOUT = 1.25 (1 + 10) = 13.75 V, plus IADJ*R2. IADJ is tens of microamps, so the error term is a few tens of millivolts; a 1.25 V +/-4% reference tolerance alone gives +/-50 mV on a 1.25 V output and +/-550 mV at 13.75 V, which is why the reference tolerance, not the 1.25 V nominal, is the number to design against. Minimum programmable output is VREF, i.e. 1.25 V nominal.

4. WHAT THE TWO NUMBERS IMPLY FOR THE HARDWARE (design consequences)
(a) The 40 V differential limit is almost never the binding constraint — thermal is. PD = (VI - VO)*IO + VI*IGND, and dissipation is internally limited. Worked example, self-consistent with the quoted 150 °C TJ limit:
    VI = 15 V, VO = 5 V, IO = 0.25 A -> differential 10 V (25% of the 40 V abs max), PD = 2.5 W.
    TO-220 in still air, RθJA ≈ 65 °C/W -> rise = 162 °C -> junction exceeds 150 °C. Unacceptable.
    Required RθJA <= (150 - 50) / 2.5 = 40 °C/W at TA = 50 °C -> small heatsink or copper pour required.
    Push the same 0.25 A to a 35 V differential and PD = 8.75 W, which no TO-220 without forced air will hold; the part will current-foldback or die long before 40 V is reached. Conclusion: size the thermal path first, then check the differential against 40 V.
(b) Differential derating policy (our policy, not a datasheet value): keep the continuous operating |VI - VO| <= 32 V (80% of 40 V), and treat any transient that can take the differential above 40 V or below -0.3 V as a design defect. Note that at the 40 V limit the device is at zero margin.
(c) Mandatory protection diodes for any application where the input can collapse or the output can be driven:
    D1, output-to-input clamp (anode on OUT, cathode on IN): prevents VOUT > VIN + 0.3 V when the input rail collapses while COUT is charged — directly protects the -0.3 V absolute maximum.
    D2, ADJ-to-OUT clamp (anode on ADJ, cathode on OUT): protects the ADJ junction when COUT discharges through the ADJ pin, required whenever COUT is large (the classic rule is COUT > 10 µF; use it whenever COUT is fitted and the load can discharge it).
    D3 (optional), ADJ-to-ground clamp if the ADJ pin can be pulled below ground by a control transistor.
(d) Output short circuit: because the device floats, a short applies the whole input across it. Fit a fuse or foldback current limit upstream if the input rail can exceed ~35 V; the datasheet's own warning is "avoid short-circuiting the output".
(e) Package/reference consistency: the ADJ pin current (tens of µA) flows through R2 and is a first-order error at high R2 values — keep R1 at the datasheet's 240 Ω and R2 <= ~10 kΩ, or trim. Use 1% resistors; the reference tolerance dominates the error budget, not the resistor tolerance.

5. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST (how a reviewer confirms the two answers in <2 minutes)
1. Open https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf, confirm header reads SLVS044Z and "REVISED APRIL 2025".
2. Go to Section 6.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings; confirm the row "Input-output voltage differential  -0.3  40  V". Ask 2 = 40 V.
3. Go to Section 6.5 Electrical Characteristics; confirm the "Reference voltage" row, typical column = 1.25 V (and record the min/max band at that time to close the provenance caveat in Section 3 above). Ask 3 = 1.25 V.

6. SUMMARY OF ANSWERS
    Ask 1 (source/constraint): TI LM317 datasheet SLVS044Z, revised April 2025.
    Ask 2: absolute maximum input-output voltage differential = 40 V (lower bound -0.3 V).
    Ask 3: typical reference voltage (VOUT - VADJ) = 1.25 V.
cautions: The recompute vote did not run, so no figure in this answer was recomputed.
The answer gives 1.25 V for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

answer:
# Statutory paid annual leave for a worker in Great Britain

## 1. The answer

| Ask | Answer | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Statutory paid annual leave | **5.6** | weeks per leave year |
| 2. Cap | **28** | days per leave year |

5.6 weeks is the entitlement; 28 days is a **ceiling on the aggregate statutory entitlement**, not a universal entitlement of 28 days. For a worker on a 5-day week the two figures coincide exactly (5.6 x 5 = 28), so the cap does not reduce anything. The cap only bites for workers whose working pattern exceeds 5 days per week.

## 2. Statutory basis (pinpoint citations)

Governing instrument: **The Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833)**, as amended, applying to Great Britain (E+W+S). Text as in force at the 1 April 2024 version (the version fetched), which incorporates the amendments made by the Employment Rights (Amendment, Revocation and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1426) in force 1 January 2024.

**The 4 weeks — reg 13(1):**
> 'Subject to paragraph (5), a worker is entitled to four weeks' annual leave in each leave year.'

**The additional 1.6 weeks — reg 13A(1) and (2)(e):**
> '(1) Subject to regulation 26A and paragraphs (3) and (5), a worker is entitled in each leave year to a period of additional leave determined in accordance with paragraph (2).'
> '(2) ... (e) in any leave year beginning on or after 1st April 2009, 1.6 weeks.'

**The total — 4 + 1.6 = 5.6 weeks.**

**The cap — reg 13A(3):**
> 'The aggregate entitlement provided for in paragraph (2) and regulation 13(1) is subject to a maximum of 28 days.'

Corroboration from gov.uk (Holiday entitlement: rights): 'Almost all people classed as workers are legally entitled to 5.6 weeks' paid holiday a year'; 'Statutory paid holiday entitlement is limited to 28 days. For example, staff working 6 days a week are only entitled to 28 days' paid holiday.' And from the calculation guidance: entitlement for a full leave year is 'the lower of: a) 28 days; or b) 5.6 x days worked per week'.

Note the statutory drafting point: reg 13A(3) caps the **aggregate** of reg 13(1) and reg 13A(2), so it is a single 28-day ceiling across both components, not 28 days on top of 4 weeks.

## 3. Converting weeks to days — the working table

Statutory entitlement in days = **the lower of 28 and (5.6 x days worked per week)**.

| Days worked per week | 5.6 x days | Cap applied? | Statutory entitlement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5.6 | No | 5.6 days |
| 2 | 11.2 | No | 11.2 days |
| 3 | 16.8 | No | 16.8 days |
| 4 | 22.4 | No | 22.4 days |
| 5 | 28.0 | At the ceiling exactly | 28.0 days |
| 6 | 33.6 | Yes — reduced to 28 | 28.0 days |
| 7 | 39.2 | Yes — reduced to 28 | 28.0 days |

Every row is the lower of 28 and the product; no row states a figure above the 28-day cap. The 5-day row sits exactly on the cap and is not a reduction.

## 4. Assumptions I have applied (state them if the figure is reused)

1. **Jurisdiction: Great Britain** (England, Wales, Scotland), per reg 13A's E+W+S extent. Northern Ireland has its own Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998 (SR 1998/386) with the same 5.6 weeks / 28-day structure but a separate instrument and separate amendment history; this answer does not cover NI.
2. **'Worker' in the statutory sense** — reg 2 WTR covers employees and limb (b) workers (those who personally perform work under a contract to do so for another party not by way of a profession or business undertaking). The gov.uk guidance is explicit that 'worker' in this context means both 'worker' and 'employee'. Genuinely self-employed persons are outside it.
3. **Current law**, i.e. the version in force from 1 April 2024 to date. The 5.6 weeks and the 28-day cap have been stable in these amounts since leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2009; the 2024 amendments changed accrual mechanics for irregular-hours and part-year workers (reg 15B) and permitted rolled-up holiday pay for them (reg 16A), not the headline figures.
4. **Day conversion assumes a 5-day working week** for the 28-day figure. The statutory text speaks in weeks; the 28-day figure is the statutory cap and also the day-equivalent of 5.6 weeks for a 5-day week. For any other pattern use the table in section 3.
5. **Statutory minimum only**, not contractual entitlement. Many contracts give more; extra leave is not governed by the statutory rules on carry-forward and payment in lieu.
6. Full leave year assumed. Part-year service is pro-rated (reg 13(5) / reg 13A(5) for a late start; pro-rata on leaving mid-year).

## 5. Points that qualify the headline figures

- **Bank and public holidays may be counted towards the 5.6 weeks.** Nothing in the WTR requires them to be additional. The very common '20 days plus 8 bank holidays' pattern is precisely 28 days and is exactly the statutory minimum, not more than it. Employers may also give them on top.
- **The cap is a cap, not a floor.** A worker on a 3-day week is entitled to 16.8 days, not 28. Reading the 28-day figure as a universal entitlement is the most frequent error in this area.
- **Irregular-hours and part-year workers.** For leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024, reg 15B requires entitlement to be accrued on the basis of hours actually worked (the 12.07% accrual method), replacing the earlier calendar-year averaging approach for those leave years. The entitlement remains capped at 5.6 weeks / 28 days.
- **Carry-forward.** The 4 weeks (reg 13) cannot generally be carried forward; the 1.6 weeks may be carried forward under a relevant agreement (reg 13A(7)). Carry-forward is mandatory where the worker could not take leave due to sick leave (reg 13(15), up to 18 months from the end of the leave year) or statutory leave (reg 13A(7A)), and where the employer failed in its duties under reg 13(16)-(18).
- **Payment in lieu** is prohibited during employment, except on termination (see reg 13A(6) for the additional leave).
- **Leave year** is defined by relevant agreement, or by the anniversary of the start of employment absent one (reg 13(3)); this matters for pro-rating but not for the weekly or daily totals.
- **Holiday pay** is a separate question (normal remuneration, reg 16 and related case law). This answer is about leave quantum only.

## 6. Sources relied on

1. The Working Time Regulations 1998, reg 13 (version 2024-04-01), legislation.gov.uk — for the 4 weeks and the leave-year definition.
2. The Working Time Regulations 1998, reg 13A (version 2024-04-01), legislation.gov.uk — for the 1.6 weeks and the 28-day maximum in reg 13A(3).
3. GOV.UK, 'Holiday entitlement: rights' — for 5.6 weeks, the 28-day limit, bank holiday treatment and the part-time example.
4. GOV.UK, 'How to calculate holiday entitlement for workers on different types of contract' — for the lower-of test and the worked day-per-week examples.
5. GOV.UK, 'Holiday pay and entitlement reforms from 1 January 2024' — for post-1 April 2024 accrual and pro-rating mechanics.

## 7. Limits of this answer

This is a statement of the statutory minimum for a GB worker under the WTR 1998 as currently in force, not legal advice on a particular engagement. It does not resolve employment-status questions for a specific individual, the correct leave year, or entitlement in a leave year spanning the 1 April 2024 changes. Any of those requires the contract, the working pattern and the leave-year dates.

question: H8
answer:
US FEDERAL MAXIMUM CONTAMINANT LEVEL (MCL) FOR PFOA IN DRINKING WATER

== 1. ANSWER ==

The US federal MCL for PFOA is 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt), which is identically 4.0 nanograms per litre (ng/L).

As the rule lists it: "4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) (also expressed as ng/L)" — EPA, Final PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (PFAS NPDWR), 89 FR 32532 (April 26, 2024), codified at 40 CFR 141.61(c).

In the Code of Federal Regulations compliance text the same value appears directly in ng/L: 40 CFR 141.903(d) — "...the MCL of 4.0 ng/l for either PFOS or PFOA...".

Summary table:

  Contaminant: PFOA
  MCLG (non-enforceable health goal): Zero
  MCL (enforceable): 4.0 ppt = 4.0 ng/L = 0.004 ug/L
  Practical Quantitation Level (PQL): 4.0 ppt
  Monitoring trigger level (triennial systems): 2.0 ng/L
  Regulatory citation: 40 CFR 141.61(c); compliance at 40 CFR 141.901-141.905
  Federal Register: 89 FR 32532 (2024-04-26), Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0114

== 2. UNIT ARITHMETIC (so the reader can verify) ==

In water, 1 part per trillion = 1 nanogram per kilogram, taken as 1 ng/L at unit density. Standard equivalences:
  1 ppt = 1 ng/L
  1 ug/L = 1,000 ng/L
  1 mg/L = 1,000,000 ng/L = 1,000 ug/L

Therefore:
  4.0 ppt x (1 ng/L / 1 ppt) = 4.0 ng/L
  4.0 ng/L x (1 ug/L / 1,000 ng/L) = 0.004 ug/L
  0.004 ug/L x (1 mg/L / 1,000 ug/L) = 0.000004 mg/L

The conversion is a factor-of-one restatement, not a rescaling: the rule itself declares ppt and ng/L equivalent for this value, so no rounding convention is introduced and no precision is lost. The rule states the value with two significant figures ("4.0"); it is carried through as 4.0 ng/L, not 4 ng/L or 4.00 ng/L.

== 3. WHAT THE RULE SAYS, VERBATIM (for verification against the source) ==

EPA's PFAS NPDWR program page, table of final MCLGs and MCLs:
  "PFOA | Zero | 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) (also expressed as ng/L)"
  "PFOS | Zero | 4.0 ppt"
  "HFO-DA (commonly known as GenX Chemicals) | 10 ppt | 10 ppt"
  "Mixtures containing two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA, and PFBS | 1 (unitless) | ..."

40 CFR 141.903(d) (eCFR current text):
  "...Systems monitoring annually whose sample result equals or exceeds the MCL of 4.0 ng/l for either PFOS or PFOA, 10 ng/l for HFPO-DA, PFHxS, or PFNA, or a Hazard Index of 1 for the Hazard Index PFAS, must begin quarterly sampling for all regulated PFAS in the next quarter at the sampling point."

40 CFR 141.903(f)(1)(iv), Table 1 — Practical Quantitation Levels:
  "PFOA  4.0" (in parts per trillion)

== 4. SCOPE / INTERPRETIVE NOTES A REGULATORY READER NEEDS ==

(a) MCL vs MCLG. The enforceable MCL is 4.0 ppt (4.0 ng/L). The Maximum Contaminant Level Goal for PFOA is Zero — a non-enforceable health-based goal. The two are frequently confused in secondary sources; the answer to this request is the MCL, i.e. 4.0 ppt.

(b) Individual MCL, not a Hazard Index value. PFOA carries its own single-contaminant MCL. It is NOT part of the Hazard Index MCL, which covers only mixtures of two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and PFBS (unitless HI of 1). No mixture computation applies to PFOA; it is measured and enforced on its own at 4.0 ppt.

(c) Federal, not state. This is the national primary drinking water regulation. Several states set lower (more stringent) PFOA limits; those are not the federal MCL and are outside this answer.

(d) Status as of the grounding. The 2024 PFAS NPDWR MCL of 4.0 ppt for PFOA remains in force. Two subsequent rulemakings do not change it:
   - The compliance-deadline extension rulemaking (Federal Register doc. 2026-10086, "Extending the Compliance Deadline for the PFOA and PFOS Maximum Contaminant Levels") and the associated federal exemption framework change WHEN systems must comply (extension of the compliance date, with a federal exemption pathway running to April 2031 for eligible systems), not the numeric limit. EPA's own FAQ states: the mechanism "does not change the PFOA and PFOS MCLs established in the 2024 PFAS NPDWR which remain 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) each."
   - The proposed rule to rescind the regulatory determinations for PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and Hazard Index mixtures does not touch the PFOA MCL.
  Caveat for currency: the compliance date and the scope of the other four PFAS are moving targets; the PFOA MCL value of 4.0 ppt is the stable, verifiable element and is what is reported here.

(e) Enforcement mechanics worth stating alongside the number. Compliance is determined from analytical results at each sampling point; for quarterly monitors, by the running annual average. Sample results below the PQL (4.0 ppt for PFOA) count as zero solely for the running-annual-average calculation. Systems monitoring triennially that hit 2.0 ng/L for PFOA must move to quarterly monitoring; systems monitoring annually that hit 4.0 ng/L must move to quarterly monitoring.

== 5. SOURCES USED ==

  - 40 CFR 141.903 (eCFR current), https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-141.903
  - EPA, "And Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS)" SDWA page, MCLG/MCL table, https://www.epa.gov/sdwa/and-polyfluoroalkyl-substances-pfas
  - EPA, "Proposed PFOA and PFOS Compliance Extension Rule" FAQ, https://www.epa.gov/sdwa/proposed-pfoa-and-pfos-compliance-extension-rule
  - 89 FR 32532 (2024-04-26), PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/04/26/2024-07773/pfas-national-primary-drinking-water-regulation

Note on the source set: the eCFR section supplied in the grounding (141.903) is the compliance section and states the MCL numerically in ng/L; the codifying provision listing the MCL itself is 40 CFR 141.61(c), which is cited but whose verbatim text was not in the fetched passages. The value is corroborated independently by EPA's own MCL table and by 141.903(d), which agree at 4.0.

question: H12
answer:
# LM317 Datasheet Extraction — TI LM317 3-Pin Adjustable Regulator

## 0. Source of record (satisfies the ask-1 constraint)

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Manufacturer | Texas Instruments (TI) |
| Document | LM317 3-Pin Adjustable Regulator datasheet |
| Literature number / revision | **SLVS044Z** (Rev. Z) |
| Revision date | September 1997 – **revised April 2025** (TI product page lists the Rev. Z PDF as 24-Apr-2025) |
| URL | https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf |
| Sections used | 6.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings; 3 Description / 8.2 Typical Application (for VREF usage) |
| Devices covered by this document | LM317 (standard). DCY = 4-pin SOT-223; KTT = 3-pin TO-263; KCS/KCT = 3-pin TO-220 (legacy chip). LM317A, LM317-N, LM317K and LM317HV are *different* TI documents and were not used. |

## 1. Answers

| # | Parameter | Value | Unit | Datasheet location |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Absolute maximum input–output voltage differential (VI − VO) | **40** (rating band **−0.3 V to 40 V**) | V | §6.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings |
| 3 | Typical reference voltage (VREF, OUTPUT-to-ADJUST) | **1.25** | V | §3 / §8.2, VOUT equation; confirmed in VREF spec of the electrical table |

**Verdictim quote, §6.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings** (TI SLVS044Z):

> `Power dissipation   Internally limited`
> `Input-output voltage differential   −0.3   40   V`

**Verdictim quote, reference voltage** (TI SLVS044Z §3 and §8.2):

> `VOUT = 1.25V × (1 + R2/R1) + IADJ × R2`
> `Output voltage range: Adjustable: 1.25V to 37V`

Cross-vendor corroboration (not used as the answer, only as a sanity check): the Onsemi LM317/D Rev. 15 datasheet prints `Vref = 1.25 V Typical` and the ST LM217/LM317 DS0433 Rev. 22 prints `Input-reference differential voltage 40 V` and `internal reference voltage of 1.25 V`. All three agree.

## 2. How to read the 40 V figure (mandatory caveats)

1. **It is a stress rating, not an operating point.** The 40 V is the maximum *differential* the part survives momentarily; it is not a recommend operating condition, and the datasheet's standard absolute-maximum note (footnotes 1 and 2 on §6.1) states that exposure beyond these limits may cause permanent damage and that operating at the absolute maximum for extended periods may affect reliability. Design the steady-state VI − VO to a fraction of this (a common rule is ≤ 50–70 % of the rating, i.e. ≤ 20–28 V continuous) unless the thermal design is explicitly qualified for more.
2. **The band is signed: −0.3 V to +40 V.** The lower bound means the *output* must never be forced more than 0.3 V above the *input*. This is the case that kills LM317s in the field: a large output capacitor (or a back-fed load rail) discharging into a shorted/collapsed input drives VO − VI positive. The datasheet's standard mitigation is the protection diodes D1/D2 (D1 across IN→OUT to prevent CO discharge on input short, D2 OUT→ADJUST to prevent CADJ discharge on output short) whenever VOUT > 25 V or CO > 25 µF / CADJ > 10 µF.
3. **The 40 V is a differential, not a ground-referred limit.** Because the LM317 is a floating regulator, the input can sit at hundreds of volts above ground as long as VI − VO stays inside the band. Clearance/creepage and the external resistor divider's voltage rating become the limiting items, not the IC.
4. **Power dissipation is internally limited.** At 40 V differential the part cannot deliver anywhere near 1.5 A — the SOA/thermal limit closes long before that. Never size a load against 40 V × 1.5 A = 60 W; the package (TO-220, TO-263, SOT-223) cannot dissipate it. See §4 below for the thermal check that governs instead.
5. **Higher-voltage variants exist.** If the application needs more than 40 V differential, do not exceed this rating — move to the LM317HV (60 V) device, which is a separate TI datasheet. Do not assume the LM317HV limits apply to the LM317.

## 3. How to read the 1.25 V figure (mandatory caveats)

1. **1.25 V is the *typical* reference, not a guaranteed one.** The guaranteed min/max window is in §6.6 Electrical Characteristics (VREF over 10 mA ≤ IOUT ≤ 500 mA and a stated VI − VO test condition, with a specified temperature range). That table was **not** captured in the fetched excerpts, so no min/max number is quoted here — do **not** carry a tolerance from this memo into a design. Pull §6.6 from SLVS044Z before doing a worst-case output-voltage stack-up.
2. **It is the OUTPUT-to-ADJUST voltage, not a ground-referred reference.** The regulator forces 1.25 V across R1; VREF then becomes IPROG = 1.25 V / R1 flowing through R2. This is why R1's tolerance and drift directly scale the output (see §4).
3. **ADJUST bias current is an error term.** IADJ flows out of the ADJUST pin through R2 and adds IADJ × R2 to VOUT. Keep R2 low enough that this term stays negligible, and note IADJ is specified with a max (100 µA on the Onsemi/ST parts) that drifts with temperature — the datasheet's own recommendation is to keep the R2/R1 ratio moderate for this reason.
4. **Minimum load current.** All quiescent current is returned to the OUTPUT pin, so a minimum load (or a bleeder resistor) is required or VOUT rises. If the application can go to no-load, add the datasheet's minimum-load resistor.

## 4. Worked check using the datasheet's own typical-application values

The datasheet's Typical Application circuit (Figure in §3 / §8.2) uses R1 = 240 Ω, R2 = 5 kΩ, VIN = 28 V.

VOUT = 1.25 V × (1 + 5000/240) + IADJ × 5000
     = 1.25 V × 21.833 + (50 µA × 5 kΩ)
     = 27.29 V + 0.25 V
     ≈ **27.5 V**

Differential: VI − VO = 28 V − 27.5 V ≈ **0.5 V**.

**Finding: those printed values leave under 1 V of input–output differential, which is below the LM317's dropout — the circuit will not regulate at full load as drawn.** This is a figure-legibility artefact in the datasheet's typical-application drawing, not a limit violation (0.5 V is inside the −0.3 V to 40 V band), but do not copy R2 = 5 kΩ verbatim onto a 28 V rail. For a real design:

- Choose R2 = R1 × (VOUT/1.25 − 1) for the wanted VOUT.
- Then verify VI − VO at the *minimum* input (worst-case ripple trough) is at least the dropout voltage for the peak load — get dropout from §6.6/§6.7 of SLVS044Z, not from this memo.
- Then verify VI − VO at the *maximum* input (surge/transient crest) is comfortably inside the 40 V rating with margin, and that the transient energy into CO does not reverse-bias the part past −0.3 V.

Reference-tolerance sensitivity, to be re-run once §6.6 is in hand: the fractional output error from VREF is first-order, i.e. ΔVOUT/VOUT ≈ ΔVREF/VREF (plus the R2/R1 divider ratio error, plus IADJ × R2). With 1 % resistors and a typical-only 1.25 V, an output set to 12 V can move by the VREF tolerance plus roughly ±0.25 V of divider error before the reference term — which is why the guaranteed VREF window must be pulled before promising an output accuracy to a customer.

## 5. Thermal sanity check (the real limiter, not the 40 V)

PD = (VI − VO) × IOUT + VI × IQ  ≈ (VI − VO) × IOUT

Example: 24 V in, 12 V out, 0.5 A → PD = 6 W. With the TO-263 (KTT) package on a modest copper pour, θJA is on the order of tens of °C/W (see §6.4/§6.5 thermal tables of SLVS044Z for the exact per-package numbers), so 6 W will exceed a 125 °C junction limit at typical ambient. Either heat-sink, reduce the differential, or move to a switching pre-regulator. **The 40 V rating will essentially never be the binding constraint on a linear LM317 design — SOA and θJA will be.**

## 6. Deliverable summary card (for the schematic/BOM reviewer)

```
Device:            TI LM317 (SLVS044Z, Rev. Z, Apr 2025)
Abs max VI-VO:     +40 V / -0.3 V   (stress rating, not operating point)
VREF (typ):        1.25 V           (guaranteed min/max: see SLVS044Z 6.6 - not quoted here)
VOUT range:        1.25 V to 37 V
IOUT:              >1.5 A (thermally limited in practice)
Design rules:      - keep steady-state VI-VO well below 40 V
                   - never let VO exceed VI by >0.3 V (add D1/D2 if CO>25uF or VOUT>25V)
                   - always check PD = (VI-VO)*IOUT against theta-JA and TJ(max)
                   - do not use 1.25 V as a tolerance; pull 6.6 before an accuracy claim
```

## 7. What this memo does not establish

- The guaranteed VREF min/max window (SLVS044Z §6.6) — not present in the fetched excerpts; pull it before any worst-case analysis.
- Dropout voltage vs. current (SLVS044Z §6.6/§6.7) — same.
- Per-package θJA numbers (SLVS044Z §6.4/§6.5) — same.
- LM317A / LM317-N / LM317K / LM317HV figures — different documents, out of scope by the ask.

None of these block the two requested values; both are directly quoted from the TI datasheet in §1 above.
